```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(knitr)
  library(psych)
  library(DT)
})
out <- "funnel_out"
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(out, "FINDINGS.csv")))
rd <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(out, f), show_col_types = FALSE)

manifest   <- rd("01_scoring_manifest.csv")
membership <- rd("01_score_membership.csv")
scores     <- rd("01_participant_scores.csv")
measure    <- rd("02_measurement.csv")
cfa        <- rd("02c_cfa_model_summary.csv")
cfa_load   <- rd("02d_cfa_loadings.csv")
efa_load   <- rd("02e_efa_loadings.csv")
parallel   <- rd("02b_parallel_analysis.csv")
fcors      <- rd("02h_cfa_factor_correlations.csv")
cfa_cmp    <- rd("02i_cfa_model_comparisons.csv")
airef_k    <- rd("02j_airef_efa_k_comparison.csv")
desc       <- rd("03_descriptives.csv")
findings   <- rd("FINDINGS.csv")
sens       <- rd("07_sensitivity.csv")

lab <- setNames(manifest$display_label, manifest$scale)
lab["art_net_real_minus_fake (prior exposure)"] <- "ART net"
lab_s <- setNames(paste0(manifest$instrument, ": ", manifest$display_label), manifest$scale)
lab_s["art_net_real_minus_fake (prior exposure)"] <- "ART net (real − fake authors)"
headline_order <- manifest$scale[manifest$tier == "headline"]
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
show <- function(d, ...) kable(d, ...)
# Text filters only: numeric columns would get slider filters, whose JS library
# is not reliably embedded, and the table then fails to draw.
long_table <- function(d) datatable(mutate(d, across(where(is.numeric), as.character)),
                                    rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
                                    options = list(pageLength = 15, scrollX = TRUE, ordering = FALSE))
n_main <- nrow(scores)
q17_n <- findings |> filter(startsWith(family, "Q:")) |> pull(n) |> max()
item_id <- function(x) str_extract(x, "^[^:]+")
```

This report reads the outputs of `funnel.R` (`Rscript funnel.R` first). It
re-estimates nothing except the WSE factor-count checks in
@sec-wse, which are fast and not saved by the funnel. Everything here is
exploratory and post hoc: n = `r n_main`, one sample, no replication
(Q17 tables and plots use n = `r q17_n`; see §1).

For the before-and-after comparison with the old 18-script pipeline, see
`explain/README.md` and the figures in `explain/`.

# 1. From cleaned data to the analysis sample

- **Sample:** `r n_main` participants with complete records on all four
  surveys, session order, and the Author Recognition Test (ART). That n is
  used in every table and plot unless a caption says otherwise.
- **Q17:** AI-tool use is available for `r q17_n` of those `r n_main` (one
  straight-line Q17 submission is excluded). Q17 analyses and plots are
  n = `r q17_n`.
- **Sessions:** each participant wrote once alone and once with an LLM, in
  counterbalanced order (`r sum(scores$sess_order == "Traditional_First")`
  Traditional_First, `r sum(scores$sess_order == "AI_First")` AI_First).
  IMI and WSE were answered after the writing-alone session; Beliefs about AI
  and AI Reflection after the AI session.
- **Scoring rules, applied once:**
  - IMI reverse-worded items (3, 4, 13, 15, 18) arrive already reverse-scored.
  - Beliefs cost items (17-20) arrive reverse-coded; they are flipped back
    once so a high score means more perceived cost, as in Chan & Zhou.
  - WSE was a 0-100 slider with five stops (0/25/50/75/100), mapped exactly
    to 1-5.
- **No items are dropped.** Every score is the plain mean of its items
  (not a factor score).

# 2. Measurement decisions

## 2.1 The rule: CFA when a structure exists, EFA when it does not

| Survey | What the source did | Our check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Beliefs about AI (Chan & Zhou, 2023) | Three separate CFAs (Knowledge, Value with three facets, Cost); no EFA "due to this strong theoretical basis"; scored item totals; Pearson r | CFA, replicating their three models, plus combined models | A theory-defined structure exists, so we test it |
| IMI (Ryan; Deci & Ryan) | Subscale means; "investigators perform their own factor analyses on new data sets" | CFA of the three subscales; EFA as a supplement | The subscales are long established (McAuley, Duncan & Tammen, 1989, used CFA) |
| WSE / PSWSES (Schmidt & Alexander, 2012) | Exploratory PCA with varimax, three components; every analysis used the overall mean | EFA, factor-count checks, omega hierarchical | Their groups were descriptive, so there is no tested structure to confirm |
| AI Reflection (local) | No source | EFA only, comparing 1-3 factors | Custom scale; its groups came from our own EFA on this sample, so a CFA would only re-fit that EFA |

KMO is a screen for EFA only; it is not a CFA requirement.

## 2.2 KMO and the old pipeline's gate

```{r kmo}
measure |>
  transmute(Survey = instrument, Items = p,
            `Pearson KMO` = f3(kmo_pearson),
            `Polychoric KMO` = if_else(is.na(kmo_polychoric), "not estimable", f3(kmo_polychoric)),
            `Smallest eigenvalue (polychoric)` = f3(min_eig_poly)) |>
  show()
```

The old pipeline stopped Beliefs at "KMO below .50". The polychoric matrix
for Beliefs has a negative eigenvalue: the pairwise estimates contradict each
other, because Knowledge answers pile up at the top (66% at the maximum).
Inverting a near-broken matrix makes KMO collapse for every item at once.
The Pearson KMO on the same data is `r f2(measure$kmo_pearson[measure$instrument == "Beliefs"])`.
The gate was reacting to an estimation problem, not to unrelated items, and
it led to dropping the whole Knowledge block.

## 2.3 CFA results

```{r cfa}
cfa |>
  transmute(Model = model, Factors = factors, Items = p, df,
            CFI = f3(cfi), TLI = f3(tli), RMSEA = f3(rmsea), SRMR = f3(srmr),
            `MLR CFI` = if_else(is.na(mlr_cfi), "NA", f3(mlr_cfi)),
            `MLR RMSEA` = if_else(is.na(mlr_rmsea), "NA", f3(mlr_rmsea)),
            Note = note) |>
  show()
```

How to read this table:

- **WLSMV** (ordinal) is the primary estimator. **MLR** treats answers as
  numbers and is a sensitivity check. WLSMV CFI runs optimistic at N = 82.
- **SRMR** under .08 means the model reproduces the observed correlations
  well (Hu & Bentler, 1999). **RMSEA** runs high when a model has few
  degrees of freedom and the sample is small (Kenny, Kaniskan & McCoach, 2015).
- Our Chan & Zhou replications have the **same degrees of freedom** as theirs
  (5, 41, 2), so they are the same models. Their SRMRs were .026, .040, .019
  with N = 405.
- Every WLSMV model warns that the parameter covariance matrix is not
  positive definite. There are more sample statistics (thresholds plus
  polychoric correlations) than participants, so standard errors are
  approximate; loadings and fit are still usable.

### Is splitting worth it? Nested comparisons and factor correlations

```{r cfa-cmp}
cfa_cmp |>
  transmute(`Simpler model` = simpler, `More factors` = more_factors,
            `Chi-square difference` = f2(chisq_diff), `df difference` = df_diff,
            p = signif(p, 2)) |>
  show()
```

A nested chi-square test nearly always favors more factors, so the factor
correlations decide whether a split is meaningful. Above roughly .85, two
factors are not separable in this sample (Brown, 2006).

```{r fcors}
fcors |>
  filter(model %in% c("imi_3", "beliefs_6")) |>
  transmute(Model = model, Pair = paste(factor_1, "x", factor_2),
            r = f2(r), `95% CI` = paste0(f2(ci_low), " to ", f2(ci_high))) |>
  show()
```

- **Beliefs value facets:** Attainment, Intrinsic and Utility correlate
  .83-.93, and Attainment-Utility's interval reaches 1. Value is one headline
  score; the facets are detail-tier.
- **IMI:** .44-.59, clearly separable. Three headline scores.
- **AI Reflection:** no CFA; see @sec-airef.

## 2.4 IMI: does the EFA find the official subscales?

```{r imi-efa}
imi_efa <- efa_load |>
  filter(instrument == "IMI") |>
  select(item, item_text, MR1, MR2, MR3)
imi_efa |>
  mutate(across(c(MR1, MR2, MR3), f2),
         `Official subscale` = case_when(item <= 7 ~ "Interest", item <= 13 ~ "Competence", TRUE ~ "Effort")) |>
  rename(Item = item, Statement = item_text) |>
  show()
```

Without being told the groups, the three-factor EFA recovers the official
subscales for 17 of 18 items. Item 13 ("This was an activity that I couldn't
do very well", reverse-scored) splits evenly between two factors and is the
weakest CFA loading
(`r f2(cfa_load$std_loading[cfa_load$model == "imi_3" & cfa_load$item == "i13"])`).
The IMI's .60 loading rule describes how its developers built the
subscales, not an instruction to delete items. We keep item 13 and check
that nothing depends on it:

```{r item13}
s13 <- sens |> filter(str_detect(variant, "item 13")) |>
  mutate(version = if_else(str_detect(variant, "without"), "without 13", "with 13"),
         other = lab[str_remove(variant, ".* x ")]) |>
  select(version, other, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = version, values_from = estimate)
s13 |> transmute(`Competence correlated with` = other,
                 `With item 13` = f2(`with 13`), `Without item 13` = f2(`without 13`),
                 Change = f2(`without 13` - `with 13`)) |>
  show()
```

## 2.5 WSE: one total or three subscales? {#sec-wse}

```{r wse-k}
W <- read_csv("data_raw/WritingEfficacy_Wide.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)[, -1] / 25 + 1
names(W) <- as.character(1:20)
Rw <- suppressWarnings(polychoric(W, global = FALSE, correct = 0.5, smooth = FALSE))$rho
k_fit <- map_dfr(1:4, function(k) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(fa(Rw, k, n.obs = 82, fm = "minres", rotate = "oblimin", smooth = FALSE))
  tibble(`Factors (k)` = k, RMSEA = f3(f$RMSEA[1]), TLI = f2(f$TLI), BIC = round(f$BIC))
})
map_k <- which.min(suppressWarnings(vss(Rw, n = 5, n.obs = 82, fm = "minres", plot = FALSE))$map)
om <- suppressWarnings(omega(Rw, nfactors = 3, n.obs = 82, plot = FALSE, fm = "minres"))
show(k_fit)
```

| Criterion | Suggests |
|---|---|
| RMSEA / TLI reach common cutoffs (RMSEA <= .05, TLI >= .90) | 3 factors |
| Parallel analysis | `r parallel$parallel_k[parallel$instrument == "WSE"]` factors |
| BIC (penalizes complexity) | 1 factor |
| Velicer's MAP | `r map_k` factor |
| Omega hierarchical (share of the total score due to one general factor) | `r f2(om$omega_h)`; ECV `r f2(om$ECV)` |

The criteria disagree, which is itself the finding: there is no crisp
subscale structure. Omega hierarchical of about .6 means one dominant general
factor with real but smaller subfactors. Rules of thumb (Reise and
colleagues) treat roughly .70-.80 as essentially one thing. Combined with the
source authors scoring only the total, the 20-item mean is the headline WSE
score (alpha `r f2(manifest$alpha[manifest$scale == "w_total"])`). The
subscales stay in the detail tier, using the published groups adjusted so
each item sits in one group; `explain/WSE_Group_Versions.csv` compares them
with EFA-derived groups.

## 2.6 AI Reflection: how many factors? {#sec-airef}

```{r airef-k}
airef_k |>
  transmute(`Factors (k)` = k, RMSEA = f3(rmsea), TLI = f2(tli), BIC = round(bic),
            `Factor correlation` = if_else(is.na(max_factor_r), "", f2(max_factor_r))) |>
  show()
```

AI Reflection was written for this study, so there is no published structure
to confirm. Its two groups came from the old pipeline's EFA on these same
participants; a CFA would only re-fit that EFA, so the factor count is
compared within EFA.

Evidence is mixed and we do not treat 2 as confirmed. In this sample,
parallel analysis suggests
`r parallel$parallel_k[parallel$instrument == "AIRef"]`
factors while BIC, TLI and RMSEA improve at 3. The old pipeline (n = 91,
including salvage cases) pointed the other way: parallel analysis suggested
3, but BIC and TLI favored 2, and the third factor rested mostly on one item.
The 3-factor split is not stable across samples (here it pulls the two
"I was satisfied" items apart, with item 1 loading .93). The 2-factor split
is the same in both samples: items 1-3 (process: satisfied, enjoyed, easy)
vs items 4-12 (learning and the final summary). We keep 2 for that
cross-sample stability and a readable process/product reading — not because
fit prefers it. Fit is modest at every k; both scores are exploratory and
study-specific.

# 3. The scores

Each score is the **mean of its items**. Tiers were fixed from measurement
quality **before** looking at correlations.

Three checks:

1. **Defined** — source subscale, or clear item wording for the local AI Reflection scale.
2. **Separable** — not glued together by very high factor correlations in this sample.
3. **Reliable** — internal consistency usable as a score (alpha reported below).

**Headline** = pass all three. **Detail** = fail at least one (still scored; used only in the appendix map).

```{r scorecard}
scorecard <- tribble(
  ~scale, ~defined, ~separable, ~reliable_note, ~fails,
  "b_knowledge",  "yes (Chan & Zhou)", "yes (single factor)", "alpha ok", "",
  "b_value",      "yes (Chan & Zhou)", "yes (facets collapsed)", "alpha ok", "",
  "b_cost",       "yes (Chan & Zhou)", "yes (single factor)", "alpha ok (lower)", "",
  "b_intention",  "yes (Chan & Zhou)", "yes (2 items)", "alpha ok", "",
  "b_attainment", "yes (Chan & Zhou facet)", "no (r .83–.93 with other value facets)", "alpha ok", "separable",
  "b_intrinsic",  "yes (Chan & Zhou facet)", "no (r .83–.93 with other value facets)", "alpha ok", "separable",
  "b_utility",    "yes (Chan & Zhou facet)", "no (r .83–.93 with other value facets)", "alpha ok", "separable",
  "i_interest",   "yes (IMI)", "yes (CFA r .44–.59)", "alpha ok", "",
  "i_competence", "yes (IMI)", "yes (CFA r .44–.59)", "alpha ok", "",
  "i_effort",     "yes (IMI)", "yes (CFA r .44–.59)", "alpha ok", "",
  "w_total",      "yes (authors scored total)", "yes (one total)", "alpha ok", "",
  "w_process",    "weak (PCA groups, not CFA)", "mixed (factor-count criteria disagree)", "alpha ok", "defined / separable",
  "w_physical",   "weak (PCA groups, not CFA)", "mixed (factor-count criteria disagree)", "alpha ok", "defined / separable",
  "w_timeeffort", "weak (PCA groups, not CFA)", "mixed (factor-count criteria disagree)", "alpha low", "defined / separable / reliable",
  "a_process",    "yes (item wording: process)", "yes (stable 2-factor split)", "alpha ok", "",
  "a_product",    "yes (item wording: product)", "yes (stable 2-factor split)", "alpha ok", "",
  "a_total",      "no (part–whole of both headline parts)", "n/a", "alpha ok", "defined"
)
desc |>
  left_join(manifest |> select(scale, display_label, tier, items), by = "scale") |>
  left_join(scorecard, by = "scale") |>
  arrange(desc(tier == "headline"), match(instrument, c("Beliefs", "IMI", "WSE", "AIRef"))) |>
  transmute(Tier = tier, Survey = instrument, Score = display_label, Items = items,
            Mean = f2(mean), SD = f2(sd), Alpha = f2(alpha),
            Defined = defined, Separable = separable, Reliable = reliable_note,
            `Fails (if detail)` = if_else(fails == "", "—", fails),
            `At ceiling` = paste0(round(100 * pct_items_at_max), "%")) |>
  show()
```

Old pipeline names stay in parentheses on some labels. Knowledge has a strong
ceiling, which limits how strongly it can correlate with anything.

Exact item statements (filterable):

```{r membership}
membership |>
  arrange(desc(tier == "headline"), match(instrument, c("Beliefs", "IMI", "WSE", "AIRef")), scale, item) |>
  transmute(Tier = tier, Survey = instrument, Score = display_label, Item = item, Statement = item_text) |>
  long_table()
```

# 4. Headline map

Every cell is a Spearman correlation between two **item-means** (not factor
scores). Labels mix source-defined subscales (Beliefs, IMI, WSE total) and
the EFA-stable AI Reflection process/product means. Axis labels already
prefix the survey. Caption on the figure: n = `r n_main`.

![](funnel_out/plots/Headline_Correlation_Map.png)

Faded cells are within-survey pairs (context only; not tested). Stars mark
family B: 35 cross-survey headline pairs, BH and Bonferroni within that
family.

Cross-survey pairs that survive BH, sorted by rho (same information as the
starred cells; no second Score A / Score B table):

```{r family-b-bars, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
b_hits <- findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "B:"), survives_bh) |>
  mutate(pair = paste0(lab_s[predictor], "\n× ", lab_s[outcome]),
         pair = factor(pair, levels = pair[order(estimate)]),
         star = if_else(survives_bonf, "**", "*"))
ggplot(b_hits, aes(estimate, pair, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(estimate), star),
                hjust = if_else(estimate >= 0, -0.15, 1.15)), size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8",
                       midpoint = 0, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.55, 0.85),
                     breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.6, 0.2),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rho", y = NULL,
       title = "Headline cross-survey hits",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; * survives BH; ** survives Bonferroni (family B)")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8, lineheight = 1.05),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 14, 10))
```

## Comparison with Chan & Zhou (Pearson r with Intention)

```{r family-a}
src <- c(b_knowledge = .179, b_value = .603, b_attainment = .587,
         b_intrinsic = .456, b_utility = .502, b_cost = -.301)
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "A:")) |>
  transmute(Score = lab_s[predictor],
            `This sample` = f2(estimate),
            `Chan & Zhou (N = 405)` = f2(src[predictor]), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2)) |>
  show()
```

n = `r n_main` here.

Value, its facets, and Cost replicate in direction and size. Knowledge runs
the opposite way, likely helped by its ceiling; treat it as a divergence.

# 5. Author Recognition Test

**ART net** = number of real authors recognized minus number of fake-author
foils endorsed. It indexes prior print exposure, not an outcome of the AI
session. False alarms are rare
(`r round(100 * mean(scores$art_fake_false_alarms == 0))`% of participants
picked none), so hits and net are nearly the same number.

```{r art-table}
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "D:")) |>
  arrange(p_bh) |>
  transmute(Score = lab_s[predictor], `rho with ART net` = f2(estimate),
            `95% CI` = paste0(f2(ci_low), " to ", f2(ci_high)),
            `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Verdict = verdict) |>
  show()
```

```{r art-heatmap, fig.width = 6.2, fig.height = 5.2}
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "D:")) |>
  mutate(score = factor(lab_s[predictor], levels = rev(lab_s[headline_order])),
         star = case_when(survives_bonf ~ "**", survives_bh ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")) |>
  ggplot(aes("ART net\n(real − fake)", score, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(estimate), star)), size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Spearman\nrho") +
  labs(x = "ART net (real authors − fake foils)", y = "Headline score (survey: name)",
       title = "Headline scores × ART net",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; * survives BH; ** survives Bonferroni (10 tests)")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The old scatter plots and their new versions are compared in
`explain/ART_Old_vs_New.png`.

People who recognize more authors hold less positive views of AI and rate
the AI summary's ownership and usefulness lower. These are bivariate
associations; they do not establish confounding.

# 6. Design checks: order and article topic

Question: do **average** headline scores depend on which session came first,
or on which article topic that survey followed?

Method: for each of the 10 headline scores, a Type II ANOVA with
`session order × article topic`. Topic is the article for the session that
survey followed (Beliefs and AI Reflection → AI session topic; IMI and WSE →
writing-alone topic). BH is applied within each term across the 10 scores.
Tool (AI vs alone) cannot be tested: each survey was given after only one
session type.

```{r design-checks}
dc <- rd("15_design_checks_order_topic.csv")
dc |>
  transmute(Score = lab_s[score], Term = term, F = f2(f), p = signif(p, 2),
            `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2),
            Verdict = if_else(survives_bh, "survives BH", "ns")) |>
  show()
```

```{r design-checks-note, results='asis'}
topic_hit <- dc |> filter(term == "topic", survives_bh) |> pull(score)
order_hit <- dc |> filter(term == "order", survives_bh) |> pull(score)
ix_hit <- dc |> filter(term == "order_x_topic", survives_bh) |> pull(score)
if (length(topic_hit) + length(order_hit) + length(ix_hit) == 0) {
  cat("No order, topic, or interaction term survives BH. Mean scores do not depend on which session came first or which article people got.\n")
} else {
  if (length(order_hit)) cat("Order survives BH for: ", paste(lab_s[order_hit], collapse = ", "), ".\n\n", sep = "")
  if (length(ix_hit)) cat("Order × topic survives BH for: ", paste(lab_s[ix_hit], collapse = ", "), ".\n\n", sep = "")
  if (length(topic_hit)) {
    cat("**Topic** survives BH for: ", paste(lab_s[topic_hit], collapse = ", "),
        ". That means mean levels of those scores differ by article. ",
        "The table below is **not** another headline-map ranking: it re-checks ",
        "family B/D pairs that involve those scores as **partial Spearman** ",
        "correlations controlling for topic (raw rho vs topic-controlled rho).\n\n",
        sep = "")
    if (file.exists(file.path(out, "15b_topic_partial_correlations.csv"))) {
      print(rd("15b_topic_partial_correlations.csv") |>
        transmute(`Pair involving topic-hit score` = paste(lab_s[predictor], "×",
                    if_else(outcome %in% names(lab_s), lab_s[outcome], outcome)),
                  `Raw rho` = f2(raw_rho), `Partial rho (topic controlled)` = f2(estimate),
                  `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2),
                  Verdict = if_else(survives_bh, "survives BH", "ns")) |>
        knitr::kable())
    }
  }
}
```

# 7. AI usage (Q17)

n = `r q17_n` (one of the `r n_main` analysis participants is dropped for a
straight-line Q17 submission).

**Why ChatGPT as the main tool score.** Among the `r q17_n` usable Q17 rows,
ChatGPT is by far the most-used AI tool on the checklist (rated 3+ "rarely"
or more). Grammarly is common too but is an editor, so it is excluded from
breadth. The two declared Q17 scores are: ChatGPT frequency (single 1–5 item)
and breadth (count of other tools rated 3+, Grammarly excluded). Means across
all tools, bucket proportions, and "primary model" groups are not used.

```{r q17-why-setup}
q17_long <- read_csv("09_q17_ai_use/csv/Q17_Responses_Long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(participant_id %in% scores$participant_id, !is.na(use_score))
chatgpt_tool <- "ChatGPT (including DALL-E) by OpenAI"
tool_use <- q17_long |>
  summarise(pct_use = mean(use_score >= 3) * 100, mean_score = mean(use_score),
            .by = tool) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_use))
chat_row <- tool_use |> filter(tool == chatgpt_tool)
n_use_chat <- sum(q17_long$tool == chatgpt_tool & q17_long$use_score >= 3)
q17_wide <- q17_long |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = participant_id, names_from = tool, values_from = use_score)
gram_cols <- grep("Grammarly", names(q17_wide), value = TRUE)
ai_wide <- q17_wide |> select(-participant_id, -any_of(gram_cols))
chat_v <- ai_wide[[chatgpt_tool]]
other_max <- ai_wide |> select(-all_of(chatgpt_tool)) |> apply(1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
pct_sole <- mean(chat_v > other_max) * 100
pct_tied <- mean(chat_v >= other_max) * 100
gemini_pct <- tool_use$pct_use[tool_use$tool == "Gemini (formerly Bard) by Google"]
```

ChatGPT: `r round(chat_row$pct_use)`% (`r n_use_chat`/`r q17_n`) rated 3+; mean
`r f2(chat_row$mean_score)`. Next AI tool (Gemini): `r round(gemini_pct)`%.
ChatGPT is sole highest-rated AI tool for `r round(pct_sole)`% of participants
and tied-or-highest for `r round(pct_tied)`%.

```{r q17-why-plot, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 4.5}
tool_labels <- c(
  "ChatGPT (including DALL-E) by OpenAI" = "ChatGPT (OpenAI, incl. DALL-E)",
  "Grammarly" = "Grammarly",
  "Gemini (formerly Bard) by Google" = "Gemini (Google, formerly Bard)",
  "Claude by Anthropic" = "Claude (Anthropic)",
  "Duck Duck Go AI Chat" = "DuckDuckGo AI Chat",
  "Copilot (Bing Chat) by Microsoft" = "Copilot / Bing Chat (Microsoft)",
  "DeepSeek" = "DeepSeek",
  "Meta AI (Facebook)" = "Meta AI (Facebook)",
  "GitHub Copilot" = "GitHub Copilot"
)
tool_use |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  mutate(label = unname(coalesce(tool_labels[tool], tool)),
         label = factor(label, levels = rev(label))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct_use, label, fill = tool == chatgpt_tool)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct_use)), hjust = -0.12, size = 3.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#3b73a8", `FALSE` = "#b0b7be"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 110), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "% rating tool 3+ (rarely or more)", y = NULL,
       title = "Most-used tools on Q17",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", q17_n, "; ChatGPT highlighted")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +

        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 14, 10))
```

```{r q17-table}
q17_lab <- c(q17_chatgpt = "ChatGPT frequency (1–5)", q17_breadth = "Breadth (ex Grammarly)")
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "Q:")) |>
  arrange(p_bh) |>
  transmute(Q17 = q17_lab[predictor], Score = lab_s[outcome], rho = f2(estimate),
            `95% CI` = paste0(f2(ci_low), " to ", f2(ci_high)),
            `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Verdict = verdict) |>
  show()
```

```{r q17-heatmap, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 5}
findings |>
  filter(startsWith(family, "Q:")) |>
  mutate(q17 = factor(q17_lab[predictor], levels = q17_lab),
         score = factor(lab_s[outcome], levels = rev(lab_s[headline_order])),
         star = case_when(survives_bonf ~ "**", survives_bh ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")) |>
  ggplot(aes(q17, score, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(estimate), star)), size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Spearman\nrho") +
  labs(x = "Q17 score", y = "Headline score (survey: name)",
       title = "Q17 × headline scores",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", q17_n, "; * survives BH; ** survives Bonferroni (20 tests)")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

ChatGPT × Intention is mostly a validity check: people who already use
ChatGPT say they intend to keep using AI. Breadth asks whether using more
tools beyond ChatGPT lines up with the same scores.

# 8. Item-level reading lists

Full-sample item scans (n = `r n_main`), shown before the order-split section
because splitting by session order roughly halves n.

Ranking: Bonferroni survivors first, then BH-only, then the rest; within
each, cross-session pairs first, then by |rho|. Corrections are within each
family; order only aids reading. (R) marks reverse-scored IMI items. Only
survivors are shown; full lists:
`funnel_out/10_item_x_score_ranked.csv` and `11_item_x_item_ranked.csv`.

## Items x headline scores

```{r item-score-bars, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
# Axis uses item IDs only; full wording is in the table under the plot.
# Bars sorted by |rho| for reading; rank number still matches the table order.
ixs <- rd("10_item_x_score_ranked.csv") |> filter(evidence != "not significant")
ixs_top <- ixs |>
  arrange(reading_rank) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  arrange(rho) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("#", reading_rank, "  ", score, "  ×  ", item_id(item)),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label)),
         star = if_else(str_detect(evidence, "Bonferroni"), "**", "*"))
ggplot(ixs_top, aes(rho, label, fill = rho)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(f2(rho), star),
                hjust = if_else(rho >= 0, -0.12, 1.12)), size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#bd4b3a", mid = "white", high = "#3b73a8",
                       midpoint = 0, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(min(0, min(ixs_top$rho) - 0.05),
                                max(ixs_top$rho) + 0.12),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rho", y = NULL,
       title = "Top 20 item × headline-score hits",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_main, "; sorted by rho; # = reading-list rank; full wording in table; * BH; ** Bonferroni")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 14, 10))
```

```{r item-score}
ixs |>
  transmute(Rank = reading_rank, Evidence = evidence, Sessions = session_relation,
            Score = score, Item = item, rho = f2(rho), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2)) |>
  long_table()
```

Most item-level hits come from items answered in the same sitting (Beliefs ×

# 9. Session order (does a correlation change?)

Placed last among the main sections: splitting by session order roughly
halves n (`r sum(scores$sess_order == "Traditional_First")` Traditional_First,
`r sum(scores$sess_order == "AI_First")` AI_First).

Question: does a correlation change depending on which session came first?
Each correlation is computed separately in the two order groups and compared
with Fisher's z (Spearman variance factor 1.06).

```{r order-scores}
o12 <- rd("12_order_score_x_score_ranked.csv")
o12 |>
  filter(evidence != "not significant" | reading_rank <= 5) |>
  transmute(`Score A` = a_label, `Score B` = b_label,
            `Traditional first` = f2(rho_traditional_first), `AI first` = f2(rho_ai_first),
            Pooled = f2(rho_pooled), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Evidence = evidence, Pattern = pattern) |>
  show()
```

Nearly every surviving order effect involves IMI Interest/Enjoyment with AI
attitudes. When writing alone came first, people who enjoyed it more held
less positive AI views; when AI came first, the relationship reversed.
Pooled, it looks like zero. Groups are small, levels share people and items,
and the pattern was noticed before this test was run — treat as a lead for a
planned model, not a finding.

Item-level order effects that survive correction:

```{r order-items}
bind_rows(
  rd("13_order_item_x_score_ranked.csv") |> mutate(Level = "item x score"),
  rd("14_order_item_x_item_ranked.csv") |> mutate(Level = "item x item")
) |>
  filter(evidence != "not significant") |>
  transmute(Level, A = a_label, B = b_label,
            `Traditional first` = f2(rho_traditional_first), `AI first` = f2(rho_ai_first),
            Pooled = f2(rho_pooled), `p (BH)` = signif(p_bh, 2), Evidence = evidence) |>
  long_table()
```

# Appendix A. Detail map

![](funnel_out/plots/Detail_Correlation_Map.png)

Includes the three value facets, the WSE subgroups, and the AI Reflection
total (all still item-means). Stars come from each pair's own family (B for
headline pairs, C for pairs involving a detail score). Figure caption: n =
`r n_main`.

Does the detail tier find anything the headline scores miss? Each surviving
detail correlation is listed next to its headline counterpart: the same pair
with each detail score replaced by the headline score it belongs to. The AI
Reflection total combines both headline parts, so it has no single
counterpart.

```{r detail-check}
parent <- c(b_attainment = "b_value", b_intrinsic = "b_value", b_utility = "b_value",
            w_process = "w_total", w_physical = "w_total", w_timeeffort = "w_total")
up <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% names(parent), parent[x], x)
headline_hits <- findings |> filter(startsWith(family, "B:") | startsWith(family, "D:"))
key <- function(a, b) paste(pmin(a, b), pmax(a, b))
findings |>
  filter((startsWith(family, "C:") | startsWith(family, "D2:")) & survives_bh) |>
  mutate(ha = up(predictor), hb = up(outcome),
         hit = match(key(ha, hb), key(headline_hits$predictor, headline_hits$outcome)),
         counterpart = if_else(is.na(hit), "none (AI Reflection total)",
                               paste0(lab[ha], " x ", lab[hb], ": ", f2(headline_hits$estimate[hit]),
                                      " (", headline_hits$verdict[hit], ")"))) |>
  arrange(p_bh) |>
  transmute(`Detail pair` = paste(lab[predictor], "x", lab[outcome]), rho = f2(estimate),
            Verdict = verdict, `Headline counterpart` = counterpart) |>
  long_table()
```

Every surviving detail correlation repeats a headline correlation that also
survives, at a similar size, with one exception: **WSE Process Knowledge x
ART net** (rho = `r f2(findings$estimate[findings$predictor == "w_process" & startsWith(findings$family, "D2:")])`,
BH) survives while WSE Total x ART net
(`r f2(findings$estimate[findings$predictor == "w_total" & startsWith(findings$family, "D:")])`)
does not. The old pipeline's Writing Competence factor showed the same link
(.28). It is a detail-tier lead, not a headline finding.
